speaker: The Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will cover three areas in this Statement.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: After the Second World War, many former colonies became independent countries.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In some countries, this group made up an absolute majority.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In other countries, the dominant ethnic group was the largest minority.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Many of these countries chose the language of the dominant ethnic group to be the official language of their new nations.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This is the approach of countries in the West as well, to organise themselves.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In many countries in the West, as well as elsewhere, minorities who do not speak the official language are disadvantaged.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Disadvantaged in education, employment and opportunities to progress economically and socially.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Many countries also implemented policies which favoured the dominant ethnic group at the expense of and even suppression of the minorities.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Sri Lanka is one example of this practice in the past.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Members may also access this material through the Parliamentary app.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If our founding fathers had followed the prevailing norm, Mandarin would have been our only official language.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we became independent in 1965 precisely because Mr Lee Kuan Yew and his team decided on a very different approach for Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our founding fathers took systematic steps to build a multiracial, multi-religious Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They enshrined the foundational principles: unity in diversity, justice and equality in our National Pledge.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: All citizens, regardless of race, language, or religion were to have equal status.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Policies were designed to enable each ethnic group to preserve its own cultural heritage.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At the same time, our common space would be enlarged to facilitate interaction and understanding between the ethnic groups.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Selected festivals of the major ethnicities were designated as public holidays.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And on the ground in the heartlands, activities were organised for all ethnicities to promote multiracial harmony.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This meant that we continued singing our national anthem Majulah Singapura proudly in Malay in schools and at national events.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members can see how different this approach is compared with the approach taken by most countries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We did not force any ethnic group to assimilate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The majority group accepted that while they were the biggest group, they should nevertheless take extra care and make sure that the minorities were not slighted.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was in this spirit of multicultural integration that we encouraged each ethnic group to preserve its own heritage.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we created space, space to enhance mutual understanding and develop a common identity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our founding fathers, however, faced tremendous opposition to this approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Many Chinese organisations, including some highly influential ones, asked the Government to make Mandarin our national language and the only official language.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Questions were asked: why not – since Chinese were 77% of the population?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Why should Singapore adopt English, the colonial master's language, as the language of administration and instruction?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Why should our National Anthem be in Malay?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Barisan Sosialis, the main opposition party then, took an active position on this matter.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The communist-inspired left had long relied in Singapore and Malaya on the mobilisation of Chinese-educated students and labour organisations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They did this by emphasising Chinese-language, Chinese-culture and Chinese education.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: By doing this, they repeatedly stoked tensions within the Chinese community.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The politically expedient course for the People's Action Party (PAP) government would have been to agree to these demands and make Mandarin Singapore's only official language.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It would have helped to anchor the support of the majority Chinese community.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the run-up to the 1963 General Election (GE), the PAP government's majority had been steadily whittled down.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The PAP's position did improve after the 1963 GE, but it was still in a fierce contest with the Barisan Sosialis.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Yet, it chose to follow the more difficult, more idealistic course, at a time when the PAP government needed the support of the majority Chinese population.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Lee and his colleagues chose the path that would in most contexts be seen as politically foolhardy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I would ask Members to take a moment to reflect, think about this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You will realise how extraordinary their actions were.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How this cuts against all political realities and standard norms.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And for 60 years, we have strived to achieve the ideals in our pledge.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Minorities in particular will tell you about the lived realities on the ground.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That they sometimes face racism at different levels.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Beyond what each of us hears, surveys show how minorities feel.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some Chinese will also tell you of their experiences, though the instances are much fewer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The key point however is: we set out those principles as our ideals and we swam strongly against the tide – the tide of ethnic identity as an organising principle of society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Instead, our foundational principles were a secular state, meritocracy, multiracialism, equal opportunities for all and the rule of law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A secular state, with neutral language, English, as the language of administration and instruction.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Lee explained this in this House in the year 2004: if Chinese had been made the working language in 1965, and I quote, “Singapore would fall apart.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our races would be in conflict.” And over the last 60 years, we have taken various steps to achieve the ideals in our pledge.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In this context, I will mention two key policies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These were put in place to make the ideals our reality.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The first policy, it was decided that a strong legal framework was necessary to preserve our communal harmony and minimise racial, religious conflict.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One of the first Constitutional amendments after independence established the Presidential Council for Minority Rights.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These laws take their inspiration from earlier legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They are only two among a whole framework of laws which seek to preserve our racial and religious space, and deal firmly with attacks on race, religion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: However, some Members may not be aware of them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, for their benefit, I have set out a background summary on some of these points.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we provide safe spaces where honest, frank discussions can be held.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These include, closed-door dialogues, fireside chats, regular engagements with different groups, including young people, entrepreneurs, religious groups, unions, non-profits and many others.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These settings encourage people to be rational, responsible, while pulling no punches on the substance of their views.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is, in broad terms, the first key policy underpinning our ideals.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But whilst laws can deter and penalise actions that seek to divide our society, laws alone cannot make society harmonious.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They cannot force people to understand, respect and like each other across races, religions and across divides.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These are too numerous for me to cite.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have listed some of the key examples in Annex B.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members will see that there is a fair degree of activist Government policy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the past, critics have mocked this as “social engineering” and a violation of free choice.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But today, many look at our high level of social cohesion, and ask, “What is your secret sauce?” The Economist has in the past described the Singapore Government's approach as "Dirigisme". "Dirigisme" refers to a state-led approach to economic development.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we make no apologies for our philosophy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Government also takes an active stand and approach in managing social issues, housing issues, community issues and more.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But for this approach, Singapore would not be where it is today.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have in Singapore an exceptionally high level of racial and religious harmony.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: More than 90% felt that there was sufficient involvement, or that there should be more Government involvement to ensure racial and religious harmony.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members of different communities do experience racism and face other issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The deep-seated human instinct, the tribal emotions which come from the gut, these cannot be wished away.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As the Prime Minister himself has acknowledged, it is more difficult to be a member of a minority community in Singapore than being a member of the majority communities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But as a system, we have sought to contain and overcome the natural human impulses by overlaying them with a broader sense of national identity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A community of shared values, experiences and vocabulary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And in the words in our pledge, "regardless of race, language or religion", our approach towards racial and religious issues is not to forsake our respective races, languages or religions and force a singular identity, but to forge common ground and find strength in diversity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Not perfect, but I dare say, better than most other places.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Many of these places started out better and stronger than us, but many of them have been going the wrong way.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second point, some recent incidents where race and religion have been brought into politics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The good position we have in Singapore can remain so only if Singaporeans work at keeping it that way.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Politicians, in particular, play an important role in setting the right tone for our society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Not deepening divisions, not misleading the different communities, but by encouraging constructive discussions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: By finding solutions to problems and issues faced by the different ethnic communities, not by exacerbating them and not by sharpening differences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is possible for politicians to say that they subscribe to our multiracial and multi-religious values, but still use veiled rhetoric to work up racial and religious sentiment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When one group asserts its identity aggressively, other groups in society will push back just as aggressively.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You see around the world what happens when such identity politics takes root.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Culture wars dominate US politics as parties run identity-based campaigns.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Liberals accuse the right wing of preserving white political and social dominance by portraying African Americans as sources of crime and unrest.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Republicans counter that Democrats have taken exclusionary identity politics too far, undermining traditional and nationalistic values.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Every grievance, every disagreement is framed as an ideological battle.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It becomes an all-out war with no room to compromise.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at the Netherlands, politicians openly frame Islam as incompatible with liberal Dutch values and portray themselves as protectors of Dutch culture.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some, like Geert Wilders, even go so far as to campaign around banning the Quran, closing mosques and sharpening divides for electoral gain.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We can see how societies are getting increasingly divided.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Singapore has come a long way in building harmonious, multiracial and a multi-religious society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We may look stable now, but we are no more stable than other countries, which I have cited, were before their communal relations became worse.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: With this background, let me turn to a few troubling incidents during the recent GE.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: During the last GE, one Noor Deros came to prominence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He is a self-styled preacher based in Malaysia.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He has been denied accreditation as an Ustaz here in Singapore, because he refused to comply with the Code of Ethics under Singapore's Asatizah Recognition Scheme.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He refused, despite being counselled by the Asatizah Recognition Board.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On 19 April this year, two weeks before the GE, Deros issued a public statement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He said that he would campaign for any political party which could meet his list of demands.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These demands included: one, adopting Islamic economics by changing the financial system to a non-interest-based model.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Another demand was that policies aimed at preserving existing racial proportions should be ended.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some of his demands were absurd, I would say very damaging.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, his demand that we change our financial system to be more Islamic.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This man, who is based in Malaysia, wants to stop all of that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On 23 April, Deros put up two Facebook posts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He said only the Workers' Party (WP) was taking his demands seriously.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Deros said that he would invite Muslims in Singapore to vote for WP if they agreed to his demands.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He also portrayed WP's Malay/Muslim candidate in Tampines, Mr Faisal Manap, as a more vocal champion of Malay/Muslim issues compared to Minister Masagos.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He called on Tampines voters to "do the right thing"; meaning, vote for Mr Faisal Manap.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On 24 April, Deros made further public statements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He reiterated his call for Tampines voters to vote for Mr Faisal Manap.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He also said that he had spoken to all of WP's Malay candidates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Deros was saying that he would rally votes for any political party that agreed with his demands, demands which were along racial religious lines, and he was comparing two Malay/Muslim candidates and saying, vote for Mr Faisal Manap because he has been a more vocal champion of race and religion for Malay/Muslims.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That was the main troubling issue, not whether some of his demands were absurd or whether one agrees or disagrees with his demands, or whether one agrees or disagrees with his assessment of candidates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we allow this, other racial and religious groups will have similar demands and we have to allow them to make similar calls, too.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The natural result in a democracy will be that the largest and the best-organised religions and races will get their way.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They will have the strongest lobbying power and the most number of votes, and political parties will have to listen to them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The other natural result is that the followers of different races and religions will clash.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Followers of different faiths can hold beliefs that are essentially incompatible with one another.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If different groups press their religious ideals hard, instead of compromising with one another, and if the Government prioritises the views of one faith over another, conflict is inevitable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we go down this path of canvassing based on identity politics, the result will be that most parties will appeal to the Chinese vote, and the minorities will feel the squeeze and will be marginalised.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When you try and get the Malay/Muslim vote in this way, and if the Malay/Muslim community responds, the other communities, in particular, the Chinese, will quickly notice and very likely start to view the Malay/Muslim community with suspicion, along communal lines.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is what happens in many countries and our sense is that something like that may have started to happen in Tampines.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Many Chinese voters in Tampines seem to have observed the communal nature of the appeals to the Malay voters, and they seem to have chosen to take a different direction during this GE.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But this sort of racial dynamics in politics is very bad for Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The same can happen with religions – Christianity, Buddhism, Taoism.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These will emerge as the dominant religions influencing politics that will cause deep resentment and anxiety among Muslims, Hindus and other groups.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the US now, there is a blurring of lines between religion and politics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There was an article published by Spiegel International two weeks ago on 2 October 2025.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The article reported that prominent US religious leaders are openly pushing political agendas.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One even called for the establishment of an “American theocracy” and banning Muslims from holding public office.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Instead of rejecting these ideas, some politicians in the US are promoting them in order to get votes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: More citizens have also become more accepting of political violence in the name of furthering religious ideals.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Bigger countries may possibly survive with these sorts of divisions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Singapore – we will certainly be divided, damaged and ruined.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Just consider one example from our history, which few in this House will remember.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The PAP's Malay candidates beat Singapore Umno Malay candidates in these constituencies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Umno leaders in Kuala Lumpur were furious.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They were not going to allow a non-communal party, like the PAP, make inroads into what they considered to be their special preserve.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, they launched a vicious anti-PAP and anti-Lee Kuan Yew campaign.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Malay Singaporeans who voted for PAP were called traitors.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is all it took, 10 months, to unravel everything.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Hence, when Deros started making dangerous statements, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong decided to go public.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He felt that he must respond robustly to Deros.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This was in the middle of the GE.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The statement also urged all political parties and their candidates to do their part to safeguard the harmony in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On 26 April, the Prime Minister held a press conference.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In this GE, the WP released its own statement on 26 April, the day after ELD and MHA had issued their statement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the circumstances, given the fundamentals of our multiracial, multi-religious approach and the ideals set out in our pledge, more needed to be said by WP and it needed to be said immediately after Deros had made his posts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On 23 April, Deros publicised his meeting with WP.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He said that WP were the only ones who took him seriously.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He called on all Muslims in Singapore to vote for WP if they agreed to his demands.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He also called on Tampines residents to vote for Mr Faisal Manap, specifically over Minister Masagos.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The next day, 24 April, Deros continued to speak publicly about his meeting with WP.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He said that he had met with all of WP's Malay candidates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He also repeated his call for Tampines voters to vote for Mr Faisal Manap.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Only on 26 April did WP issue its statement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That was more than two days after Deros publicised his meeting with WP and after the statement by ELD and MHA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This was during the campaign period, when every day made a huge difference.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This delay, on such an important matter, begs many questions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, sections of voters might be misled into thinking on those two days that WP was possibly considering Deros' demands.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Deros was saying all these things and WP was silent.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: MHA and ELD had to step in and say that this was unacceptable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And after that, the WP issued its statement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It said that no commitments, promises had been given and no agreements were reached.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that the WP was committed to the principle that religion and politics should be kept separate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we accept that identity politics has no place in Singapore, then a clearer and more immediate response was called for.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, something along these lines would have been much clearer: "that Deros set out various demands, based on his religious beliefs; he said that he would ask Muslims to vote for candidates who accepted his demands; he asks Muslims to vote for the WP candidates if the WP agreed to his demands; he also said that he endorses Mr Faisal Manap in Tampines, because Mr Faisal is a more vocal champion of Malay/Muslim issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The WP rejects his attempts to influence the Malay/Muslim community, based on religion and race, just as we reject his endorsement of Mr Faisal Manap, based also on religion and race.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We rejected it when he told us and we reject it now.” This is what is needed to be said.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Pritam Singh did follow up on 26 and 27 April at media interviews to say that Deros' endorsement does not mean WP will carry forward his policies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we hope that in future, if such incidents occur, there will be a more immediate, forthright and unequivocal response, given by political parties.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Establishing this common understanding on how such issues must be dealt with in future is one of the key reasons for this Ministerial Statement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I said earlier, WP fielded Mr Faisal Manap in Tampines to contest against the PAP team led by Minister Masagos.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That the Malay/Muslim vote, in particular, was being targeted was obvious, not just to Singaporeans, but pertinently, also obvious to Malaysian observers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Malaysian politicians from the Parti Islam Se-Malaysia (PAS) jumped in.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They saw an opening and urged Singaporeans to vote along racial and religious lines.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: PAS' national treasurer, Iskandar Abdul Samad, expressed support for WP's Mr Faisal Manap.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: PAS Selangor Youth chief, Mohamed Sukri Omar, reposted a social media post stating that PAP's Malay/Muslim Members of Parliament (MPs) cannot be trusted.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: More than 60 years ago, Malaysian politicians said the same things about PAP Malay/Muslim leaders then.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Its goal is to Islamise society in Malaysia.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It has persistently pushed for the adoption of Shariah law and penalties.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Does anyone, whether in here or outside, seriously believe that PAS is supporting WP's Malay/Muslim candidates in Singapore because PAS cares for Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Does anyone believe that PAS has Singaporeans' best interests at heart?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Does anyone believe that PAS subscribes to Singapore's multiracial, multi-religious model?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Statements by PAS leaders have clearly shown otherwise.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 2024, for example, the PAS President said that Mr Lee Kuan Yew's strategy of fielding candidates from diverse ethnic backgrounds had led to Malay political influence diminishing in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is why all of this reminded some of us, of the first 10 months when Singapore was part of Malaysia.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In those 10 months, between September 1963 and June 1964, the ultras managed to work up sentiments to such an extent that race riots broke out in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In Dr Goh Keng Swee's words following the 1964 riots, he feared that "Humpty Dumpty had fallen off the wall and could never be put back again." Fortunately, it was only our union with Malaysia which could not be put back together, not our multiracial country, Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It took us decades to repair the damage; decades for the scars to heal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This history is seared into some of us and it is also seared into some Malaysians, but for very different reasons.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we knew the Government had to call it out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It spoke about foreigners attempting to influence the elections.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Prime Minister also spoke about this, in his press conference on 26 April.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Foreigners targeting Singaporeans, asking them to vote on racial and religious lines.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The PAS politicians were championing one set of Malay/Muslim candidates against another set of Malay/Muslim candidates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Unfortunately, the truth is that such attempts will have some impact.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And therefore, it is incumbent on all political parties to decisively reject any attempts by foreigners to influence our election, especially on the grounds of race and religion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The WP issued a statement on 26 April.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I had also referred to this earlier, in the context of Deros.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are two concerns with WP's statement: first, on the timing; and second, on the substance.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On timing, foreign influence is a serious matter.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is even more serious in the middle of a campaign.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, given the gravity of the matter, it would have been better if WP had issued its statement immediately, without waiting until after MHA-ELD had issued their statement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What it said was that the WP had no control over what others said.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: After the WP statement was issued, Mr Pritam Singh made further statements on 26 April.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At a doorstop interview, he said that he stood behind the message in MHA-ELD's statement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It would have been better if WP had said this right from the start, responding directly and promptly to what the PAS leaders had said.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: WP did so after Prime Minister had called on all parties to make their position on foreign influence clear; and clearly and categorically reject foreign endorsements of their candidates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We hope that, in future, political parties will immediately reject any such attempt to interfere in our political process.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If this is not done immediately, clearly and unequivocally, it will give rise to questions and confusion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We therefore hope that, in future, political parties will immediately reject – and especially, when such interference is made on the basis of race and religion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will now move on to another incident during the GE.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He claimed that more opposition Malay MPs were needed to raise Malay issues in Parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What Mr Damanhuri means is more Malay "rights", more advocating for "Malay" issues, more Malay separateness.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In a separate podcast, he said meritocracy is selectively applied.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He rehashed these arguments again in rally speeches, this time in Malay.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What he is effectively doing is trading off the long-term welfare of the Malay community and our country for his immediate political gain.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is a slippery and dangerous path that will invite a strong reaction from other races in future elections.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So far, the situation has been broadly stable because the Government has anchored our country on our ideal of multiracialism.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The governing party itself has eschewed identity politics and fought against attempts to rile up the different ethnic communities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It has set out the fundamental ideals on how our society should be structured.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And it has managed to convince most Singaporeans to accept those ideals.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Meanwhile, from time to time, various parties, candidates, have tried to stir up the Chinese and Malay communities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because of the PAP government's political dominance, these efforts have not been successful.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The PAP has been the dominant political force, so, it has been able to bear the political cost of fighting against such sentiments.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Making this Statement here today, it would actually have been easier to leave all of these unsaid.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But this Statement has to be made in the country's interests.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If future generations of political leaders on all sides see such identity politics gaining traction, then they will be pressured and tempted to themselves engage in it too.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, people like Mr Damanhuri should be more honest with their constituents.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Their brand of politics will only work as long as the dominant political force, whether it is the PAP or another party in Singapore, rejects identity politics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But if people like Mr Damanhuri succeed, then the serious risk is that more and more politicians on all sides will go for identity politics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will experience the same conflicts and divisions we see unfolding elsewhere in the world.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the dangers of politicising race and religion are clear.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But that is not to say that race and religion on the one hand and politics on the other hand, are incompatible.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: All religions provide guidance on important aspects of life.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, inevitably, there will be areas where faith and public issues overlap.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Government recognises this complexity and how our identity is interwoven out of our faith, our ethnicity, our language and our culture.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In a multicultural society, a pragmatic approach of give-and-take is necessary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: People are free to practise their faiths and express views on politics and political issues, influenced by their private religious convictions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This must be done in a manner that is respectful of other religions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The public, political debate must be conducted and decided on a secular basis and there must be give-and-take on all sides.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: All political parties need to be absolutely clear.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It must never be brought into election campaigns.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Without this shared restraint, destructive competition for power and influence between the different groups can only follow.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our society is structured such that every community gives up something for the common good and every community has progressed, as the nation has progressed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If any community pushes for its interests without consideration for the other communities, then a pushback can be expected.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We need to think of our Singaporean identity as fundamental and we each have to give up something to strengthen the shared Singaporean identity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And so, when there are threats to our social cohesion, or attempts to bring race and religion into partisan and electoral politics, this Government must and will act, consistent with the principles it has upheld over the last 60 years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Statements like those from Deros and Mr Damanhuri in the last GE cannot go unaddressed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We highlighted and strongly criticised some of these instances of racial and religious politics during the GE.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we decided not to take immediate action against those who were transgressing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we cannot allow such actions to take root, because they corrode our democracy and tear our social fabric.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That deals with my second point, on recent troubling incidents which sought to bring race, religion into politics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our brand of multiracialism is not only the bridge that brings Singaporeans of all races and religions together.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it is the crux of our being as an independent nation and our continuance as a successful country.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Now that the elections are over and emotions no longer run as high, I make this Ministerial Statement to remind ourselves as Singaporeans about the framework and fundamentals that have allowed Singapore to succeed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is not the first time this House is discussing this issue, but events during the recent GE warrant this being raised again.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is too serious a matter, existential for Singapore, for us to simply let it slide.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And so, I decided to make the Statement at the earliest opportunity after the Opening of Parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is entirely understandable as long as it does not get into identity politics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we need to exercise caution that one does not get into the other.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We need to exercise caution on how these points are made.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We need to handle them with care and good sense.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Most important, we need deep commitment to our ideals.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: My Statement builds on a series of recent Government statements and speeches.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: During the election, MHA and ELD issued a strong statement warning against bringing race and religion into politics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Prime Minister also stressed that we are all Singaporeans first, regardless of our backgrounds.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the recent President's address, the President reminded us that we can never take our unity for granted and must guard it zealously.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: During the recent debate on the President's address, the Prime Minister again urged all political parties to conduct politics with seriousness, with integrity and a deep sense of responsibility.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, why do we keep repeating these points over and over again?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is because these fundamental principles are central to the very existence of Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We decided that we should state our position formally, robustly and unequivocally at the highest forum in our country – Parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The peace and harmony in our society have been the foundation for the progress we have achieved.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Since Independence, Singapore has been transformed – the physical environment, the economic opportunities, the jobs available and the standard of living.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our people's lives have improved, regardless of their race, language or religion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They have done well, not only compared to where they started out, but also compared to other communities in our region.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our multiracial model has worked and we must not heedlessly and irresponsibly put it at risk.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Generations of Singaporeans have carried the torch onward.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is much more to be done to achieve the ideals of our pledge.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it is clear, looking around the world, that we can only achieve that if we steer clear of identity politics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They chose to stay in Tanah Singapura instead and build a home here.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If they had left, we would not have remained in multiracial country as we are now.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Also, if the Chinese majority had, at that point, refused to listen to Mr Lee, then we would not be the multiracial country that we are today.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, let us remain faithful to the hopes and dreams and aspirations of our Pioneers.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Before I call hon Members for clarifications, I just wish to point out that pursuant to Standing Order No 23, Members may seek clarification on the Ministerial Statement, but no debate shall be allowed thereon.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Members can seek clarifications by way of asking questions.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I seek Members' understanding to keep your clarifications clear and concise, so that the Minister can answer as many clarifications as possible.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But before I do so, let me just read out as a preamble, a short remark that I made at the doorstop interview on 26 April, one day after the MHA-ELD statement was made.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And I said this, "I think MHA and ELD have put together a message and I stand behind that message.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We persuade Singaporeans of our value proposition and we urge all Singaporeans, regardless of race, language or religion, to judge us on our manifesto and our proposals, and what we do in Parliament for all Singaporeans, not specific communities only.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It does not refer to Noor Deros, who is a Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It makes reference to foreigners attempting to influence the GE.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This comes out on 25 April, and the Minister can correct me if I am wrong, the statement comes out at about 10.00 pm on 25 April.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I understand Minister has an issue about the context of what was said.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And the Minister concedes that on 26 April, that same day the press release of the WP was released that morning, in the evening, there is a rally, and at Tampines, I make what I think the Minister says are clearer remarks and statements about race and religion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, I have a disagreement with the Minister about the question of timing.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I am not sure whether the Minister knew him or if the Ministry knew of him, unless he was on Majlis Ugama Islam Singapura (MUIS) or had served with MUIS at some point in some capacity.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But as far as the WP is concerned, we do not really have an operations room or a Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Act (POFMA) office to monitor what foreigners or what people are saying about politics and where they may be venturing into territory which is dangerous.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But in the event there is something untoward or awry, the WP is not shy of coming together and trying to resolve the issue.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will give an example as a matter of clarification.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The first rally we had at Anchorvale, the rally site looks, starts to turn dangerous because people are slipping and sliding, and the Police commander on the ground is unsure, uncertain what is happening.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And he says, "Look, we may have to shut the rally site down".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, I said, "Let me make a remark to the crowd and ask them to keep safe".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, the point I am making to the Minister is, if something is heading into dangerous territory, I think there are many ways, in the national interest, for the Government to communicate with political parties and say, "Look, this is not on.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We need to come together, resolve it, make that clear statement".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And if the party is not prepared to make a statement, then I think the Minister is fully at liberty to make the comments that he wishes to.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Because the Prime Minister decides to take a break from the hustings and made a statement in the national interest.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, just to clarify, what considerations were on the Government's mind, in terms of trying to nip this issue at the bud?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And in my Statement, I said that the WP statement did not reject Deros' very serious conduct in asking Muslims here to support the WP on racial and religious grounds, and asking voters in Tampines to vote for Mr Faisal Manap.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I hope after the Statement we can at least have common ground that what Deros did was unacceptable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if there is common ground that that was unacceptable, then it should have been responded to immediately.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And it should have been an unequivocal rejection of what Deros said.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I said that the initial statement by WP was not clear, but it got clearer when Mr Singh gave his doorstop, and then, it became quite clear after the Prime Minister had specifically called on political parties to make their position clear.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Singh then clearly, unequivocally, rejected PAS' statements during the rally.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, on I did not say that either Mr Singh or the WP had made their position clear on Deros, it should have been made clear.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am not quite sure why there is a reference to the POFMA office or MHA or the Government, or this suggestion of should the Government have communicated with a political party in the middle of the GE.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Look, we are now here talking about Deros' meeting with the WP's Malay candidates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That means Mr Faisal Manap and four others.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Faisal Manap was and is the Vice Chairman of the WP and, if I am not wrong, probably a Central Executive Committee (CEC) member as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Faisal Manap and others need the POFMA office to tell them about their meeting with Deros and his posts?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Then, there is a larger point, a more substantive point, which I have alluded to.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Instead, what it said is that no commitments, promises or agreements had been made to Deros.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is something that you might find lawyers drafting for each other.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You do not see that in political statements, which ought to be clear and unequivocal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I think Mr Singh, if I heard him correctly, conceded that the statement could have been clearer, and I thank him for that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it should have been squarely stated that we are rejecting all of this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When there is no clear response, it raises questions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if you look at it logically, do we agree that what Deros said was serious?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think all of us, regardless of party affiliation, would agree to that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Do we agree that it required a clear and immediate rejection without any qualification and it was important to do so?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Listening to Mr Singh just now, I think he accepts that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Can the lack of a clear rejection of Deros' statement be an oversight?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Look, Mr Low Thia Khiang has described Mr Singh as "a good politician", meaning a politician who understands politics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the lack of clear response, a vague response must have been a deliberate choice based on a calculation of interests.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am just taking it point by point, as a series of logical conclusions, that there is some benefit in keeping it less clear and that Deros can swing some votes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That sort of calculation may bring some short-term benefits.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And whatever I say about Deros also goes for PAS.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But as I said, long-term damage to our country.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It goes against our National Pledge, it goes against our multiracial ideals.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, being true to our pledge has to go beyond citing it during GE rallies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It must mean putting it in practice even when it is difficult to do so.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Sincere belief requires acting true to the words of the pledge, even when it may cost some votes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I will not go into any of this detail.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I refrain from saying all of this bluntly in my speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The main purpose of my speech was to say, let us come together, keep faith with our fundamentals of multiracialism and not play identity politics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: My hope and the purpose of my speech is that we will learn from what had happened, move forward as one people, Singaporeans together, agreed on the fundamentals; close ranks when people like Deros and foreign parties like PAS try to divide us and say and agree that we will reject such attempts immediately and clearly, even if we may calculate them to be in our short-term political interest.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Let us just be clear today, we do not need to refer to the POFMA office, we do not need to refer to the Government or say the Government did not tell us.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is really what each of us is responsible for and what responsible conduct means.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When your Vice Chairman is meeting together with the slate of candidates and there are these demands, you do not need to be told by the Government, really.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I hope we can agree on these basic points.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not want to go into future hypotheticals.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What might happen in the future, we will assess the facts of each case.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And my own view on this matter is, when a nobody claims that there is a set of demands that he has of a political party, one has to think of a number of factors.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: He also later on, congratulated Prime Minister Mr Lawrence Wong.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Ultimately, in the heat of the elections, attentions are all over the place.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And for an opposition party indeed, Nomination Day – I do not think I need to state here how even the PAP had to move candidates last minute – your attention is all over the place.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But what I would say is that we had made our views quite clear on foreign interference.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I understand the Minister says that the statement on Noor Deros could have been clearer, I accept that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think we can make certain things very clear.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But my point is if we talk about the national interest, if this is so important to the Government, there are other ways to deal with it collectively as one Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: On the matter of PAS, I think the Minister made some extended comments about PAS.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: About one year ago, at this time, we know that PAP Malay MPs went to Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Malay Action Bureau in particular went to Malaysia and there was some communication with PAS, and on Petir, the PAP publication outlet, the mast head says, "The PAP story told from within". "Malaysian politics has evolved.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In the past there was only one dominant party, now there are multiple Malay parties and those with Malay components", and this is the former Malay Muslim Affairs Minister saying, "I thought it would be good for party activists to be introduced and build bridges with these parties and personalities." It is an extensive article and the Minister also said, "but I thought it would be useful to deploy our Malay activists in a way that would relive the purpose of the MAB: how do we help the party win over the Malay community now?" I am not sure what is the party's approach to this matter, but what I would be interested in is, given this relationship that the PAP and PAS seem to have, was there any attempt made by PAP Members or intermediaries in private to communicate with PAS and to inform them not to interfere in our elections forthwith?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And at the same time, did the Government make any intervention or formally raised this matter with the Malaysian counterparts as to not to do this in future?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, let us just take responsibility for it and agree that the statement that came out was not unequivocal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I think Mr Singh agrees that it should have been clearer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There should have a clear rejection of Deros' demands.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There should have been a rejection of Deros' support for WP's Malay candidates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There should have been a rejection of his support for Mr Faizal Manap.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was not done immediately and when it was done, it was done without a clear rejection.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Based on what Mr Singh agrees, in future, we need to be very aware and we need to be clear when we make our rejections.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Government should be more active, I think is Mr Singh's second point.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think we all have to work on this together, but that can only come about if we all agree on the fundamentals.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I think that then prodded WP into making clear statements on PAS but not so much on Deros.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the relationship between the PAP and PAS, Sir, there are a number of political parties in Singapore: PAP, WP, SDP, the Progress Singapore Party.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Singh knows that they all have interactions with various political parties around the world.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, let us not seek to confuse these issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is not an attempt to try and confuse the public.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The PAP can reach out to a whole variety of parties including PAS and the United Malays National Organization (UMNO), and around the region in Indonesia and other places.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is part and parcel of understanding what is going on around the world.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is very different from accepting a foreign endorsement of our candidates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Let us stick to what we are talking about here.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we are talking about how do you respond to that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I hope we can agree and move on.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think the Minister started by referring to meeting Deros and I mentioned quite clearly during the elections that he gate-crashed the meeting that Mr Faisal Manap was having with someone else.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: My understanding from Mr Faisal Manap is there was no arrangement to meet him specifically.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But this is just a fact by the by, but the points that the Minister has made in terms of not wanting such interference, rejecting individuals who attempt to use identity politics to win votes, I can agree with that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And I think most Singaporeans will agree with that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The point I wish to highlight, and I am not sure whether the Minister has been unequivocal about it, is when something like this happens, there is an asymmetry of information.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I hope the Minister can consider this in future.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But what I would like is a more unequivocal acceptance of responsibility.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I mean, however the meeting took place, Mr Deros met with five of the Member's candidates, including the Member's Vice Chairman.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, yes, there is an asymmetry of information – and that is, WP knows what happened; we do not.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We only know what Deros has put up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He knew enough to say that he is, as Mr Low described him, "a politician who understands politics".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He was able to do that after the Prime Minister called for a clear rejection.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He never did that, and WP never did that about Deros.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Let us just say that is why we waited for the elections to be over, emotions to come down, and we make the Statement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I said, I was not going to go into this level of detail, we draw a line, we move forward as one Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In future, if these things happen, the framework hopefully is clear enough, we all accept and move ahead.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you want the Government to tell you what to do and what not to do in the middle of the elections, the Government is also mindful of being seen to interfere with individual political parties.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we need to be mindful of that, because it can be politicised.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Maybe Mr Singh is welcoming of a phone call to say this is not on, but I can imagine a number of other political parties might say, you are trying to threaten me in the middle of a GE.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He said, reject this; reject identity politics, reject foreign interference.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If Mr Singh is talking about a specific reach-out to WP, we will think about it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But let us all commit, in the first place, to saying we all understand, under no circumstances is this acceptable and we will be clear in future.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Just to share that the MHA-ELD statement, again did not refer to Deros.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We do not need that sort of support.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I do not think I can be clearer than that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But the substance of what the Minister has gone on in his Ministerial Statement is not objectionable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think Mr Singh is confusing two different issues, Sir.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It also dealt with a separate issue: religion and politics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On PAS, it said something else, and then I have referred to what Mr Singh said in his doorstop and further at the rally.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On Deros, MHA-ELD statement does talk about religion and politics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It does not mention Deros, but it says religion and politics ought not to be mixed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And as I said, the WP knows, I mean, it is Noor Deros.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They met with him and he made all these demands, he made all these calls.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is all that I am saying and I think it is not a very difficult thing to agree to.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Let us not confuse that with the PAS statement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the PAS statement, I said it started out a little equivocal, then the doorstop, it became clearer, and after the Prime Minister gave his press conference at night, it was quite clear by Mr Singh.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Government dealt with the two different issues, both through the MHA-ELD statement, though it did not mention Deros, and through the Prime Minister's press conference.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I do agree that identity politics would be disastrous for Singapore, especially minorities.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, listening to the Minister's Statement, I cannot help but notice that some may interpret his Statement as suggesting that a particular group or community, in this case, the Malay/Muslim community, should bear some responsibility for allowing such sentiments to take root in the first place.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Or would he not agree with me that it is, in fact, part of a broader issue or trend that political actors, both here and abroad, are taking advantage of our racial or religious sensitivities for their own gain?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And if so, it can happen to any communities, any race, any religion or groups like new citizens.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I was not singling out any particular community.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They did not ask for these provocations nor did they support these tactics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They share the same strong commitment as any other community, to Singapore's multiracial, multi-religious approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This time, these people whom I have mentioned targeted the Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Previously in other GEs, the Chinese community has been targeted.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Those who play identity politics do not just target one community.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, after the statement by the Government was issued, MHA and ELD and the Prime Minister's press conference, many members of the Malay/Muslim communities spoke up to affirm their support for a multiracial Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In every society there will be an attempt to draw invidious comparisons to mobilise different communities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I have said in my Ministerial Statement, we have seen this in many countries and that is what was being tried in this GE – to divide Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we can see how societies are getting increasingly divided.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, let us continue to stay firm to our principles and avoid the pull of identity politics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But certainly, it is not the Malay/Muslim community that is targeted.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: But I would also like to ask the Minister to clarify if he is also saying that it would be wrong for any political party to appeal to voters based on what the party can offer to any specific community?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Or is he also saying that it would be wrong for an individual to question whether the Government has done enough for any community or to demand the Government to do more for a specific community?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, if you look at my Ministerial Statement, one of the key points is that this Government's policies over the last 60 years have benefited the minorities: Malays, Indians and others.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that if we had followed the norms set in other places in the world, minorities would have been in a far worse position.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it is entirely possible for a PAP politician to go and say the PAP is the best party to protect minority interest or protect Malay/Muslim interest, to protect Indian interest.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And it is perfectly possible for someone to counter and say that is not correct.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at the Malay/Muslim community, it has been a long-standing commitment of the PAP government to support and uplift the Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it is entirely acceptable to say or contradict that one of the Government's key policies is the upliftment of the Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is nothing wrong with advocating ways to advance a particular community or discussing legitimate community concerns.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But when we advocate for the concerns of the Malay/Muslim community or any other community, we must ensure that our advocacy is conducted responsibly in a manner that upholds Singapore's unity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, just as the Government's policies benefit the Malay/Muslim community, they must also benefit all other Singaporeans, and there is a distinction between advocating for the legitimate needs of a community versus pitting the different racial and religious groups against each other or calling on Singaporeans to vote along racial and religious lines.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I said in my speech, if you go down this route, if you go down the route that Mr Damanhuri has advocated and Deros is advocating, who will benefit?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because, ultimately, the Chinese will also suffer because we will not remain a country in the way we are.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, when raising issues that relate to particular racial or religious community, the tone matters, the setting matters.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Avoid casting every issue as an ideological battle where no compromises can be made.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Otherwise, we risk reducing our common space and inviting pushback from other communities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And never insult or belittle any racial or religious group, or attempt to pit certain groups against others.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Kenneth Tiong and Dr Charlene Chen, I have seen your hands.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Speaker, I thank the Coordinating Minister for reminding us of the importance of believing how we serve everyone and that this is a Singapore for all.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: And I also appreciate Members' appreciation of peace and harmony, being important tenets that we commit to.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: The Minister cited Mr Noor Deros and Mr Damanhuri as an illustration of attempts to bring race and religion into electoral politics.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: And furthermore, what again warrants revisiting it today?

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Was that also above and beyond incidents that we recently saw with regard to, for example, Masjid Al-Istiqamah?

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: On the "how", expanding a little bit on the hon Member's question, as well as Deputy Speaker's question, about hesitance, I wanted to highlight that minority voices may hesitate to speak up on discrimination.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: And so, how can we, as Singapore, ensure a safer space for us to be able to do that, to ensure that Singaporeans can continue to have difficult, tough but meaningful conversation on race and religion, in particular, by taking the stand of preserving mutual respect when doing so and ensuring that it is not misused or not allowed for exploitation, especially due to external forces?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: During the elections, the Government issued a statement through MHA and ELD.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Prime Minister spoke as Prime Minister, the highest level of intervention.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And he said what our principles ought to be, and he set out and asked political parties to make clear their position.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: After that, the President's speech mentioned it, the importance.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Then, the Prime Minister again spoke during the Debate on the President's speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I said in my Ministerial Statement, why are we repeating this over and over again?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Without an agreement on this basic point, Singapore will not survive.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Which is why I have pitched my speech as one that I hope all sides can agree on, as Singaporeans, and learn from, for the future.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is very important – how do we deal with such incidents in future?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I am speaking in Parliament at the earliest possible opportunity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, that answers "why now?" On the incident relating to pork, the items of meat being sent to various mosques, the matter is under investigation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Then, the Attorney-General's Chambers (AGC) will have to independently look at it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And what happens in Court, that is for the Courts to decide.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I am not speaking today because of the incidents relating to the mosque, just in case Members get that impression.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The sequence for my speech today is, as I have said: after the President's speech, this is the first occasion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And it is a speech that seeks to set out the framework and fundamentals – first, to remind ourselves; and second, to guide us for the future, for all political parties, so that we accept what is precious in Singapore and we say we will protect it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On safe spaces for minorities or for anyone, really, I mentioned it in my speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are various fora, there are young people, unions, other associations, grassroots, a variety of formats where these issues can be raised.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Nobody pulls punches on the substance of things, but they are respectful of each other.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Beyond that, if people want to organise fora on their own, they are welcome to do so and discuss these issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Two, be respectful and take the approach of "give and take".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because if you push with only your views, then others too, will push with only their views.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Remember that we are in a multiracial, multi-religious society, so approach it with common sense and give and take.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the Government will continue doing it in terms of protecting everyone, in trying to create a bigger common space.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But my speech should not be understood as saying, "Oh, you cannot speak about race or religion or discrimination or racism".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The way to deal with those is to speak about it, but do so, have a care, do so sensibly.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The Minister has set clear bars for responding to foreign influence: immediacy, categorical rejection and explicit disavowal, regardless of ambiguity or delay.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Will the Minister now apply those same standards to Michael Petraeus, the Polish national, whose "Critical Spectator" platform has published racially charged commentary on Singapore politics, including a piece titled, "WP abandons Muslim voters, turns to the Chinese"?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: His platform was previously taken down from Facebook for policy violations.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: He continues to try to influence our politics from his foreign perch, this time favouring the PAP.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Will the PAP categorically reject and disavow his support today, just as the Minister demanded that WP do so within 24 hours?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think it arises from a misunderstanding of the law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are a variety of people who have commentaries running on Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The New York Times runs articles on Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The South China Morning Post runs articles on Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And Michael Petraeus is not the only person who is a foreigner who runs commentaries, sometimes for the Government, sometimes against the Government, sometimes favouring the WP.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we took that definition, every day we will be doing nothing but taking down and trying to object to various international journals.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Hundreds of articles appear, hundreds of posts appear.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is not the Government's business to be going and censoring all of this, nor is it going to be possible.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But if there is a specific attempt to interfere in the elections and if "Critical Spectator" has put out any such post, I would welcome Mr Tiong to send it to us and we will take a look at it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As far as I know, there is not one, but I could be mistaken because I do not follow his posts and nothing has been sent to me.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Ms Hazlina, do you have a further clarification?

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim
text: I think it is important to recognise the fact that Singapore is for Singapore, and that is why we are all here today.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim
text: I was reflecting on Minister's speech on identity and what it means.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim
text: It is just a small part of what we can do and what we have to offer and who we serve.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim
text: I wanted to clarify the point about the Malay community rising above targeted intentions during hustings and actually, really seeing the unity of Singapore coming together and taking all of our identities as strengths and really serving for Singapore for all, not so much feeling victimised, but realising that while there could have been targets or attempts, it is really about coming together for what is best.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Can I invite the Member to repeat the question, because I missed part of it?

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim
text: It was more of a clarification to state that while there were potentially attempts to make the Malay community victims during hustings, falling for identity politics, we, as a community, I believe, rose above it and took the point of really coming together and realising that identity is a strength.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim
text: So, that was a point of clarification on not falling victim, but wanting to rise above it, while targeted.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim
text: Would the Minister see it in the same light?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Yes, I will agree with that description and that is, in fact, what I said as well, maybe not as elegantly as the Member.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Speaker, Sir, I would like to thank the Minister for his Ministerial Statement.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: I would just like to say that Tampines has a very diverse, yet mutually respectful community.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Our residents in Tampines would agree that Singapore's survival depends on our unity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I would say, two, or maybe three parts to this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Continue with all the policies that you see in the Annex, including the Ethnic Integration Policy, our races mixed in integrated schools and other areas, and continue to make sure our legal framework protects everyone and give everyone the confidence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Of course, everyone must feel, regardless of race, language or religion, that they are participating in the economic progress and in the social progress of Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I think something good is achieved in setting out a clear framework and heartening to hear Mr Singh say, "Yes, we could have been clearer on Deros." On timing, to me, every day matters.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He says he disagrees, but I am sure, on reflection, he will agree that during campaign, it should just have been immediate, the moment it comes out, a response.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I think we have achieved some degree of common ground, and we hope that through Statements of this nature, serious discussions in Parliament, our understanding increases.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Every Member of Parliament here goes away with a better understanding of the framework.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You will be able to talk to your grassroots leaders, to your residents and also put the points across.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And going forward, we have to continue with that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There will always be attempts to divide us, both from outside and from within, and it is up to us, each one of us, to be standing strong against it and, essentially, our society has to be given the immunity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And when the Leader of the Opposition stands up and says he agrees, then I think the immunity increases.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Speaker, I have one clarification for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, my clarification for the Minister is: would the Minister consider recalibrating that reasonable and calibrated approach that the Government has taken with racial and religious harmony in Singapore, given these findings?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Maybe perhaps it is not working for certain demographics, such as our younger Singaporeans, who may feel that safe spaces, as my fellow Member referred to, can be more open.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Because if we are constantly wary of tripping over, whether it is actual legislation or, perhaps, unseen "out of bound" markers, perhaps these conversations might not be had in the most open and respectful manner.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I listen to him, and I think it is a point he might have made in his maiden speech as well, all these fora that the Government talks about are curated, they are not "real" fora, real fora is where people come and they can speak whatever they like.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have many examples of such real fora.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Are we colonised in our mind so much that we have to continue to hark back to these theories which have failed all around the world?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What has happened in the UK, where they have all these fora that the Member has refer to?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The far right in Germany is getting into power.
